clue.text: Chancellor once again announced target

parts.note: bis is Latin for twice, called out at concerts to ask for a piece again

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we want a word that is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a mark is something aimed at

explanation.surface: A finance minister, having set a goal once, proclaims it a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: BISMARCK is said like 'bis mark'. 'Chancellor' suggests Britain's finance minister; 'once' points to the past, to Germany's first chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto von Bismarck was Germany's first Reich Chancellor, from 1871 to 1890, so a historical holder of the office.

clue.text: Perk for oldies: posh health centres in outskirts of Brussels

indicators.note: the earlier parts sit inside the edge letters
the outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the first and last letters count

parts.note: spas are resorts for health treatment

explanation.surface: Pensioners get treated to upmarket spas on the edge of the Belgian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a crossword convention. A bus pass is the free travel card Britain gives people over pension age.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus pass is a free travel benefit granted to elderly people in Britain, so a perk of old age.

clue.text: Class starts to swot, expecting test

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: Pupils begin cramming, anticipating an exam.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools a set is a group of pupils of similar ability taught together, a class.

clue.text: A question put to a dealer about paintings

parts.note: QU is the abbreviation for question

indicators.note: turned about means turned round to face the other way

explanation.surface: Someone asks an art dealer about some pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like a customer's enquiry in a gallery; the art dealer is just a seller, turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquarelles are watercolour paintings, the word coming from the French for watercolour.

clue.text: After start of church service, loves joining in to sing

indicators.note: one part follows the other in sequence
the start of a word is its opening letter
things that join in go inside, among the rest

parts.note: the Royal Navy is the senior service
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: After the church service begins, the lovers join in the hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests worship; here it is an armed service, the Royal Navy. Two loves give two O's.
explanation.definitionFit: To croon is to sing softly in a low, sentimental voice.

clue.text: At university, withhold maintenance costs

parts.note: a student who is up is in residence at university
to keep something back is to withhold it

explanation.surface: A student holds back the money owed for the upkeep of their lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Upkeep is the expense of keeping property in good repair and running order.

clue.text: Job for picket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a position of employment
second meaning: a pointed stake driven into the ground

explanation.surface: A task for a striker on the picket line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picket' suggests strikers at a gate; it is the stake of a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an appointment or position and an upright pole, as a picket is.

clue.text: Questions old people crossing a main road

indicators.note: a thing crossing another spans it from one side to the other, so it goes round it

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, the 1 written as I

explanation.surface: Elderly pedestrians making their way across a busy road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' reads as pensioners; split it into old and people. The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: An examination is a test, a set of questions put to candidates, so the noun matches 'Questions'.

clue.text: Loot criminal concealed in large building

indicators.note: something concealed in a thing is hidden inside it

parts.note: a pile is a grand house or large building
a lag is a convict, especially an old lag

explanation.surface: Stolen goods that a thief has hidden in a mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang an old lag is a habitual prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: To pillage is to plunder or rob violently, the same as to loot.

clue.text: Lost balance and suffered briefly, needing support of mate

indicators.note: said briefly, the word is cut short at the end
in a down entry, a support goes underneath, so this part comes after

parts.note: to feel pain is to suffer it
a mate is a partner, a lover

explanation.surface: Someone toppled and was briefly hurt, so needed a partner to lean on.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall over is to tumble to the ground after losing one's footing or equilibrium.

clue.text: Explain strategy to start up as market trader

definitions.meaning: first meaning: lay out one's plans and intentions plainly
second meaning, taken literally: arrange a stand of goods at a market

explanation.surface: A would-be stallholder lays out a business plan for getting started at the market.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom grew out of the literal market picture, which the clue gives as its second half.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to declare one's position or aims, as a trader displays wares on a stall for all to see.

clue.text: A child minder comes into work regularly, so it seems

indicators.note: something that comes into another word enters it and sits inside

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it steadily
a parent looks after a child

explanation.surface: A nanny seems to turn up for her job like clockwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child minder' suggests a paid nanny; here it is the parent. 'Work regularly' reads as one phrase about attendance, but it gives a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparently is the adverb for what appears to be the case, the same as 'so it seems'.

clue.text: Film about a bigwig Republican supporter's first released across the States

indicators.note: about means around, so one part wraps the next ones

parts.note: a pic is a picture, a film
a big name is a celebrity, a bigwig

indicators.note: its first letter is set free and dropped

parts.note: a fan supports a team or star

explanation.surface: A movie about a prominent Republican backer gets a nationwide release.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides in the film-industry phrase 'released across the States'. Pan-American covers all the Americas, which a strict reader might think broader than the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Pan-American means relating to all the countries of the Americas, extending across many states.

clue.text: Performer keen to make comeback

indicators.note: a comeback runs the other way, so the word is read from its end

explanation.surface: An entertainer is eager to return to the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A comeback is just what a retired star might stage, which hides that it signals turning a word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A diva is a celebrated female singer, especially in opera, so a kind of stage artist.

clue.text: Censuring revolutionary leader in Egyptian rebellion

indicators.note: one part goes inside the other
a revolution overturns the existing order, so these letters are rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Condemning the man who headed a revolt in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary leader' suggests a figure like Nasser or Che; the two words have separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurgence is an act of insurrection, a rising against established authority, so a rebellion.

clue.text: Item of clothing maybe bachelor doesn't have on

indicators.note: what a word doesn't have is left out of it

parts.note: a singleton is an unattached person, of whom a bachelor is one example

explanation.surface: A garment that an unmarried man, perhaps, isn't wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't have on' reads as 'isn't wearing'; instead the word on is dropped from the end. 'Maybe' marks the bachelor as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless vest worn as underwear or for sport, a single garment.

clue.text: Express ideas in article on wage freeze?

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part placed on another sits above it

parts.note: a pay freeze means a nil pay increase: O (zero) and RISE

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece airing views on a pay freeze.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful reading of a wage freeze as 'O rise', a rise of nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To theorise is to form and put forward theories, setting out one's speculative ideas.

clue.text: Sell top quality fish

explanation.surface: A fishmonger's slogan: sell the finest catch.
explanation.definitionFit: The vendace is a small whitefish found in a few lakes in Britain and northern Europe.

clue.text: Hostess about to pull out of business

indicators.note: to pull something out of a word is to remove it

parts.note: c is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A woman running a hotel or bar is on the verge of quitting the trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of'; split it: 'about' is one letter and 'to pull out of' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Commère is the female form of compère, a woman who presents and links the acts of a show.

clue.text: Companion on motor cycle dropping round after a bit

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away
in a down entry, a part placed on another sits above it
one part follows the other in sequence

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour
a moped is a small motorcycle

explanation.surface: A friend riding pillion loses control at the bend after a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a bit' reads as 'after a while'; 'bit' alone is the definition, as the past tense of bite. CH, Companion of Honour, is a British order.
explanation.definitionFit: To champ is to chew or bite noisily, as a horse does on its bit, so the past form matches.

clue.text: Aloud, deplore adolescent habit

indicators.note: aloud means spoken, so the words are taken by their sound

parts.note: to rue is to regret bitterly

explanation.surface: Someone loudly condemns a teenager's ingrained ways.
explanation.walkthrough: ROUTINE is said as 'rue teen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine is a regular, customary way of doing things, much as a habit is.

clue.text: Communicated with shop: Malmsey regularly to be sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up reverses its order
taken at regular intervals, every other letter is kept

explanation.surface: Someone contacted the wine shop: their Malmsey should be delivered regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: Malmsey is a sweet Madeira wine, which makes 'shop' look like a wine merchant.
explanation.definitionFit: To have emailed someone is to have sent them a message electronically, so to have communicated with them.

clue.text: A group of sailors leaving western port

indicators.note: something leaving a word departs from it, so it is taken out

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for west or western

explanation.surface: A ship's company sails away from a harbour in the west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western port' looks like one phrase for a place; 'western' is a letter to remove and 'port' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Acre (Akko) is an ancient harbour city in northern Israel, a seaport on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Dissemination of information to support African country with new leader

indicators.note: a new leader means the first letter of the country is swapped for another one

parts.note: Uganda is a country in East Africa

explanation.surface: A call to back an African nation under fresh leadership, as a political slogan might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with new leader' changes the U at the head of UGANDA, and the A that fits the crossing letters gives AGANDA. The clue does not say which letter comes in, so the grid settles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is information, often biased, spread deliberately to promote a cause or point of view.

clue.text: Disney character, you say, in silly plot

indicators.note: one part goes inside the other
something silly is muddled, so its letters are mixed up
say means spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: the letter U is said like the word

explanation.surface: You might say a cartoon character appears in a daft storyline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You say' could pass as a conversational aside; it is a homophone of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluto is Mickey Mouse's pet dog in Walt Disney cartoons.

clue.text: As Indian, move very cautiously, but not quietly

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes something, so it is taken away

parts.note: to creep is to move slowly and stealthily
p is piano, the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: Like a scout stalking prey, edge forward with care, but make some noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface leans on the old picture of the stealthy tracker; the Indian here is the people, not the movement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cree are a Native American people of central Canada, so a Cree is an American Indian.

clue.text: Adventure book's sequel abridged for circulation in plain cover, oddly

indicators.note: one part goes inside the other
letters put into circulation move around and change places
done oddly means done in a strange way, so these letters are jumbled
an abridged text is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A shortened follow-up to an adventure story goes on sale wrapped in plain paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sequel' loses its last letter and is jumbled, then goes inside a jumble of 'plain cover'. 'Oddly' looks like it asks for odd letters, but here it signals a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A picaresque novel follows a roguish hero through a string of episodic adventures, like Don Quixote or Tom Jones.

clue.text: One shouldn't be put in empty vehicle

indicators.note: what shouldn't be put in is kept out, so it is removed

parts.note: vain means empty, as in vain promises

explanation.surface: A warning that a passenger mustn't ride in an unloaded lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty vehicle' reads as a phrase about a lorry; 'empty' is the word to delete from and 'vehicle' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A van is a covered motor vehicle for carrying goods.

clue.text: One refusing to be held back

indicators.note: going back means reading the word in the opposite direction

parts.note: reined in means held in check, like a horse

explanation.surface: Someone who won't accept being restrained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held back' reads as one phrase meaning restrained; 'held' alone gives the word and 'back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A denier is a person who denies something, such as a claim or request, so one who refuses it.

clue.text: Wild dog never kept under control

indicators.note: something wild runs out of order, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A feral dog that has never been brought to heel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild dog' suggests a dingo or a wolf; 'wild' is the signal to scramble the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To govern is to rule or restrain, so something governed has been held under control.
